title: Peacocks and cranes
hookLine: the monks' monsoon poems: clouds, peacocks crying, cranes flying home

lines: WHAT THE MONKS DID WITH IT.
cards: Dark clouds stack up over the hills. Thunder. A flash of white as birds lift off a riverbank.
In the trees, a peacock cries out. Some of the brothers' songs begin right there, at the edge of the rains. The poets aren't describing the weather to pass the time.
They're telling you where they sat, and what the season did to the mind.

teach.b: First, the peacocks. In one elder's verses, peacocks with fine crests and blue necks cry out in the woods, the sky rumbles, and the wide earth is soaked with new rain. And then he says: this is the time to meditate.
The noise isn't a distraction. It's a signal. Second, the cranes.

teach.h: A WHITE CRANE FLEES THE BLACK CLOUD.
teach.b: Another elder, Sappaka, watches a crane with bright white wings take flight from a black storm cloud, afraid of it, looking for shelter. Then, he says, the river Ajakarani delights him.
He comes back to that line again and again as the birds come and go, like a song's refrain. Third, the season itself.
When the rains come, roads turn to mud, and tradition says the Buddha asked the monks to stop wandering for the rainy months and stay in one place.

teach.h: VASSA: STAY PUT FOR THE RAINS.
teach.b: That stay is called vassa, the rains retreat. So the monsoon poems are poems of staying put. The clouds move, the birds move, the river rises.
The monk doesn't go anywhere. Fourth, what these two poems leave out. They don't call the storm holy, or a trap.
They don't argue with it. They watch. A bird flies for cover.
A river runs high. A man under a roof hears it all and settles a little deeper.
The rains came. For these elders, that was enough to begin.

how: Theravada monks and nuns still keep the rains retreat, vassa, staying in one monastery for the rainy season, and lay people often visit them then with food and robes.

a pilgrimage walked at the start of the monsoon

they don't argue with it at all. they watch.

games.q: you're a monk in the forest. thunder rolls, the peacocks start crying, and the first rain hits the leaves. what do you do?
o: head for the village before the roads turn to mud.
sit down: the poem says this is the time to meditate.
wait for the noise to stop before you begin.
games.why: in the elder's verses, the peacocks cry, the sky rumbles, the earth is soaked, and he says: this is the time to meditate. the noise is the signal.

practice: Go to a window, step outside, or just close your eyes and feel the air, and watch what the sky is doing without calling it good or bad.

If a bird crosses, follow it until it's gone; if a sound comes, a car, a gust, a door, let it be the peacock's cry, a signal to come back to the breath. And stay where you are, the way the monks stayed for the rains.

wordCard.voice: Vassa. The rains, and the rains retreat: the season behind the brothers' rain songs, peacocks crying as the clouds come in, a white crane flying for shelter ahead of the storm. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: vassa, the rains, and the rains retreat when monks stay in one place.

carryVoice: Your line: the rains came. The monks stayed put, and watched. That's day seven hundred ninety-nine.
